title: Inheritance
summary: Build specialised types on top of a general one, and let each supply its own behaviour.

steps.title: Building on a base class
body: A savings account is an account with something extra. Copying the whole `Account` class and adding to it would mean fixing every bug twice.
**Inheritance** lets one class start from another:
public decimal Balance { get; protected set; }
public void Deposit(decimal amount) { Balance += amount; }
public void AddInterest() { Balance += Balance * InterestRate; }
- `: Account` means *a `SavingsAccount` is an `Account`*. `Account` is the **base** class, `SavingsAccount` the **derived** class.
- The derived class gets everything the base has (`Owner`, `Balance`, `Deposit`) and adds its own members.
- `protected set` is the access level from the last lesson finally earning its place: derived classes may set `Balance`, outside code may not.
A class can have only **one** base class.

steps.prompt: Using the classes from the card, which line does **not** compile?
steps.explain: Inheritance flows one way. A savings account has everything an account has, but a plain account knows nothing about interest.

steps.title: Constructors and base(...)
body: Constructors are **not** inherited. If the base class needs data to be valid, the derived constructor must pass it up with `base(...)`.
public SavingsAccount(string owner, decimal rate) : base(owner)
`: base(owner)` runs the `Account` constructor **first**, then the body of the `SavingsAccount` constructor. So the base part is always valid before the derived part starts.
Any checks in the base constructor still apply. A derived class cannot skip them.

steps.prompt: Build a `Manager` that is an `Employee` with a team size. Put the property before the constructor.
lines: public Manager(string name, int teamSize) : base(name)
also: public Manager(string name, int teamSize) : base(name)
steps.explain: The base class is named after the colon on the class line. The constructor passes `name` up with `: base(name)` and stores only what is new.

steps.title: virtual and override
body: Often a derived class needs to do the same job **differently**. The base class marks a method `virtual` (*you may replace this*), and the derived class replaces it with `override`.
public virtual decimal Premium() { return BasePrice; }
public override decimal Premium() { return BasePrice + 50m; }
Here is why it matters. A variable of the base type can hold any derived object, and the call goes to the **object's** version:
So code that loops over a `Policy[]` works for every kind of policy, including kinds written next year. Inside an override, `base.Premium()` calls the version you replaced.

steps.prompt: One loop, three kinds of policy. What does this print?
code: public virtual decimal Premium() { return BasePrice; }
public override decimal Premium() { return BasePrice + 50m; }
public MotorPolicy(decimal basePrice, int pastClaims) : base(basePrice) { _pastClaims = pastClaims; }
public override decimal Premium() { return base.Premium() + _pastClaims * 100m; }
steps.explain: The variable `p` is typed `Policy` every time, but each call runs the override belonging to the actual object. `MotorPolicy` reuses the base answer and adds 100 per past claim.

steps.title: Standard and express
prompt: - constructor `Shipment(decimal weightKg)`, stored in a `get`-only property `WeightKg`
- overrides `Cost()`: the standard cost plus 10. Call `base.Cost()` rather than repeating the formula.
starter: // Cost(): 5 plus 2 per kg, and derived classes may replace it
template: Dojo.Eq("a 0 kg Shipment costs 5", 5m, new Shipment(0m).Cost());
Dojo.Check("ExpressShipment inherits from Shipment", typeof(ExpressShipment).BaseType == typeof(Shipment), "Declare it as: class ExpressShipment : Shipment");
Dojo.Eq("ExpressShipment keeps WeightKg from the base class", 3m, dojoExp.WeightKg);
Dojo.Eq("through a Shipment variable, the express price is still used (35)", 35m, dojoAsBase.Cost());
hints: The base method needs the word `virtual`: `public virtual decimal Cost() { ... }`
The derived class starts `class ExpressShipment : Shipment` and its constructor ends with `: base(weightKg) { }`.
The override is `public override decimal Cost() { return base.Cost() + 10m; }`

steps.title: Abstract classes
body: Sometimes the base class is only an idea. *An employee* gets paid, but there is no sensible default for how much: it depends on the kind.
Mark the class `abstract` and it cannot be created with `new`. Mark a method `abstract` and it has **no body**: every derived class is forced to supply one.
`YearlyPrice` is written once, in the base, and calls a method that does not exist yet. Each derived class fills in `MonthlyPrice` and gets `YearlyPrice` for free.
`virtual` says *you may override*. `abstract` says *you must*. If you forget, the compiler tells you.

steps.prompt: Complete the abstract base and one plan that derives from it.
steps.explain: A method with no body must be `abstract`. The derived class names its base after `:`, passes constructor data up with `base(...)`, and supplies the method with `override`.

steps.title: ToString and sealed
body: Every class you write already has a base class: `object`. That is where `ToString()` comes from, and it is `virtual`, so you can override it.
`Console.WriteLine(money)` and `$"{money}"` both call `ToString()` for you. Without an override you get the class name, which helps nobody reading a log.
Nothing can inherit from a sealed class. Use it when a class was not designed to be extended. That is most classes, and it stops surprises later.

steps.prompt: One class overrides `ToString`, the other does not. What does this print?
code: public override string ToString() { return "#" + Text; }
steps.explain: The `ToString` inherited from `object` just returns the type's name. `Label` replaces it, and both `WriteLine` and string interpolation pick up the override.

steps.title: Sidekick piece: reports
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** `sk list` and `sk list --time` print reports. They share a frame (a title, an underline, then lines) and differ only in their lines. That is a base class with one abstract method.

- `public string Render(IReadOnlyList<TaskItem> tasks)`: the title, a line of `-` as long as the title, then every line; `(nothing yet)` instead when there are no lines. Lines joined with `\n`, no newline at the end.

**`class OpenReport : Report`**: title `Open tasks`; one line per task that is not `Done`: `SK-001  Fix login redirect` (code, two spaces, title), plus `  ~0h 45m` when it has an estimate, plus `  (timer running)` when its timer runs.

**`class LoggedReport : Report`**: title `Time logged`; one line per task with logged minutes: `$"{Ids.Format(t.Id)}  {t.Title,-30} {Sk.FormatMinutes(t.LoggedMinutes),8}"`, then a total line `$"{"Total",-38} {Sk.FormatMinutes(total),8}"`. No total when there are no lines.
Your `TaskItem` and `Ids` from this module and `Sk.FormatMinutes` from First steps are ready to use. Collect the lines in a `List<string>` and finish with `string.Join("
", lines)` (a `StringBuilder.AppendLine` would add Windows line endings).
solution: var lines = new List<string> { Title, new string('-', Title.Length) };
template: var dojoTasks = new List<TaskItem> { new TaskItem(1, "Fix login redirect", 45), new TaskItem(2, "Write docs"), new TaskItem(3, "Review PR", 20), new TaskItem(4, "Plan demo", 60) };

Dojo.Eq("the open report", "Open tasks
----------
SK-001  Fix login redirect  ~0h 45m
SK-002  Write docs
SK-004  Plan demo  ~1h 00m  (timer running)", new OpenReport().Render(dojoTasks));

Dojo.Eq("the time report", "Time logged
-----------
SK-001  Fix login redirect               1h 30m
SK-003  Review PR                        0h 25m
Total                                    1h 55m", new LoggedReport().Render(dojoTasks));
Dojo.Eq("an empty open report", "Open tasks\n----------\n(nothing yet)", new OpenReport().Render(new List<TaskItem>()));
Dojo.Eq("no time logged: no total", "Time logged\n-----------\n(nothing yet)", new LoggedReport().Render(new List<TaskItem> { new TaskItem(9, "Fresh") }));
Dojo.Eq("a report you have never seen uses your Render", "Done\n----\nReview PR", new DojoDoneReport().Render(dojoTasks));
Dojo.Check("Report is abstract", typeof(Report).IsAbstract, "write abstract class Report");
Dojo.Check("both reports are a Report", new OpenReport() is Report && new LoggedReport() is Report, "inherit with : Report");
foreach (var t in tasks) if (t.Done) lines.Add(t.Title);
public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
public static bool TryParse(string text, out int id)
hints:
`Render`: `var body = Lines(tasks);` then a list starting with `Title` and `new string('-', Title.Length)`, then `(nothing yet)` or `AddRange(body)`, joined with `
`.
In `OpenReport.Lines`, skip done tasks with `continue`, and build the extras with `t.EstimateMinutes > 0 ? $"  ~{Sk.FormatMinutes(t.EstimateMinutes)}" : ""`.
`LoggedReport.Lines` keeps a running `total` and adds the `Total` line only when `lines.Count > 0`.
steps.explain: `Render` is written once in the base class and calls `Lines`, which each report fills in. The tests' own `DojoDoneReport` proves it: a report you never wrote gets your frame for free.
